title: Is Gulf oil rebound at risk as US-Iran war enters uncharted waters?
gist: Gulf oil exports through Hormuz are rebounding as markets bet the worst of the US-Israel-Iran war is over and Washington shifts to de-escalatory rhetoric after the midterms, but experts warn the uneasy stalemate is unlikely to be durable given pressure on both sides.

insights.claim: Oil keeps flowing through the Strait of Hormuz and Gulf exports are rebounding as markets cautiously bet the worst of the US-Israel-Iran war is over, despite continued Iranian claims of attacks.
insights.speaker: Samuel Wendel
insights.so_what: Market is pricing de-escalation; downside volatility if that bet breaks.
insights.quote: markets cautiously bet that the worst of the US-Israel-Iran war is over

insights.claim: The feared post-midterm US offensive has not materialized, although the US struck Iran's Qeshm Island this month, and Washington's rhetoric has shifted toward de-escalation.
insights.speaker: Samuel Wendel
insights.so_what: Reduced near-term probability of a major US offensive.
insights.locator: Although the US military has launched strikes

insights.claim: Optimism about a diplomatic opening may prove short-lived amid signs the current status quo is unsustainable.
insights.speaker: Samuel Wendel
insights.so_what: Investors should not extrapolate calm; tail risk of breakdown remains material.
insights.quote: Any such optimism, however, may prove short-lived amid signs the current status quo is unsustainable.

insights.claim: Energy Aspects' Richard Bronze said the stalemate can persist for a while but is unlikely to be durable long-term given pressure on both sides, with no firm timeline for a breakdown.
insights.speaker: Samuel Wendel
insights.so_what: Hold optionality on oil upside; timing of a breakdown is unknowable.
insights.quote: The stalemate can persist for a while but is unlikely to be durable in the long term given pressure on both sides
